newsitem.title: USA: U.S. businessmen say wage gains not inflationary.
newsitem.headline: U.S. businessmen say wage gains not inflationary.

text.p: U.S. wage gains are not powerful enough to create inflation and thus do not warrant a "pre-emptive" interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve, U.S. business owners told Reuters this week.

The owners, who serve or have served on the business advisory councils to Federal Reserve regional banks and whose businesses employ between 65 to 450 workers, say productivity gains, partly driven by the difficulty of raising prices on the goods and services they produce, mean any higher wages they pay are not likely to be passed on to consumers.

"(My employees') wages are up and it's my job to see that their productivity is up by giving them better tools and systems to work with," said William Braun, president of Custom Rubber Corp in Cleveland.

With price pressures not in evidence in any of the official consumer or producer price indices, the phenomenon most often cited to argue the case for a Federal Reserve rate hike is that tight labor markets will lead to higher wages that in turn will lead to higher prices.
But even in a comeback city like Cleveland, Customer Rubber is located in a core urban area where there is a pool of unemployed people seeking work, Braun said.
"We can still find workers. We haven't had to raise wages to bring new personnel into our door," he said.

Barbara Roberts, president of FPG International, a New York City-based photo agency with 250 employees and 41 affiliated companies around the world, said beginning wages at her firm have risen 3.5 percent to four percent in the last year, not so much because of a tight labor market but because her growing firm needs workers with more credentials.
"I very much feel that it's not necessary for the Fed to raise interest rates," said Roberts, chairman of the Business Advisory Council of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
Roberts said many factors are curbing wages and prices.
"I see a lot of very qualified 40-year-olds out of work and displaced Wall Street people taking jobs at lower salaries than they once had," she said.
Using the Internet can also cut costs, said Roberts.
"The Internet is a very efficient, less expensive way to market and advertize products," she said. "If you can cut those costs, there's less need to raise your prices."
Businesses can also use the Internet to purchase equipment or services they need at lower prices, Roberts said.
"If you get conversant with the various Web sites that sell things like high-end computer equipment, you can save a ton of money," she said.
"You have to look at all the new stuff that is happening and if you sum it up, you have a pretty anti-inflationary theme," Roberts concluded.
One segment of the workforce that saw wages rise in the last six months was workers at the minimum or low end of the wage scale.

Peter Ten Eyck, president of Indian Ladder Farms, an apple orchard 12 miles from the New York State capital Albany, has 100 people on his payroll during the course of a year. When the minimum wage went up last year, people in the agricultural business in New York State had to give commensurate increases to their workers, Ten Eyck said.
But Ten Eyck doesn't expect that his workers' higher wages will be reflected in the cost of his apples to consumers.
"As far as the need for raising interest rates, I say no," said Ten Eyck. "You've got to get leaner and meaner because apples are selling for the same prices," he said.

Big farms can improve productivity by using expensive machinery. At smaller farms, wider profit margins come from adding value. Ten Eyck's Indian Ladder Farms has a cider mill and sells the cider it makes directly to the public.
"It's a game of inches," said Ten Eyck. "You have to do a thousand little things and do each of them right."

Ten Eyck also said the "soft costs" of his payroll have fallen. New York State worker compensation premiums, which run from $12 to $43 for every $100 of agricultural payroll, "actually went down in absolute dollars," he said.
Ronald Cohen, senior partner at Cohen & Co, a Cleveland-based regional C.P.A. firm, does not think the Fed needs to raise rates when there are no signs of inflation.
"We can monitor inflation closely enough so we don't have to guess when to pre-empt it," he said.

As far as the labor market is concerned, Cohen said he sees "plenty of unemployed people, but their skills do not necessarily meet the needs of the job." Cohen said wage increases at his firm are modest and "seem to be offset by productivity gains, thanks to technology."

Central Ohio, where Scott Rusch is vice president and treasurer of Anomatic Corp which has 450 employees who manufacture and supply anodized aluminum components for cosmetic containers, is located in the proverbial tight labor market. There the unemployment rate is 3.5 percent.
"People are hard to find and the ones that you do find are often short on the training for the positions you're trying to fill," Rusch said.
To retain most of its workers and to attract new people, Anomatic's total wage and benefit costs have increased four to 4.5 percent over the last year, Rusch estimated.
But those increased compensation costs have not translated into higher prices for its products, primarily due to price competition from overseas markets where labor is cheap.
That leaves the onus on business owners "to get that productivity up to match the higher wages," said Busch.
Busch said the Fed doesn't have to raise rates now.
"We are not able to raise prices," he said. "People will not accept price increases. And suppliers are holding down prices on what we buy. I don't see inflation out there."
